Tentative Ruling:
This is a lemon law action. On 3/23/2021, Plaintiffs Kari Dubont and Joshua Jensen
purchased a new 2021 GMC Sierra 1500 (the "Subject Vehicle") sold with express warranties
from Defendant General Motors (or "GM"). It was sold with defects and nonconformities that
manifested during the applicable warranty period. None of the repairs performed by Defendants’
representatives permanently repaired the defects. GM has failed to replace the Subject Vehicle
or promptly make restitution as required under the Song-Beverly Act (the “Act”). The operative
Complaint, filed 2/18/2025, asserts 5 causes of action:
(1) Violation of the Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act § 1793.2(d)
(2) Violation of the Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act § 1793.2(b)
(3) Violation of the Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act – Breach of Express Warranty
(4) Violation of the Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act – Breach of Implied Warranty
(5) Violation of Business and Professions Code § 17200
Plaintiffs now move for an award of $21,460 in attorney’s fees and $899.20 in costs and
expenses for a total of $22,359.20 as the stipulated prevailing party in this action pursuant to a
settlement agreement. (Dillavou Decl., ¶4, Exh. 1, the “Settlement Agreement”). Pursuant to the
settlement, Defendant agreed to pay Plaintiffs $51,500, including a payoff of the vehicle loan
balance, plus “reasonable attorneys’ fees, costs, and expenses pursuant to subdivision (d) of
Section 1794 of the Civil Code as determined by the Court,” and expressly stipulated that
“Plaintiffs are the prevailing party for the purposes of said fee motion.” (Id. at ¶5.) Plaintiffs assert
GM maintains a blanket policy requiring a fee motion whenever requested fees exceed $5,000
regardless of case complexity or time expended. (Id. at ¶6.) Plaintiffs even offered to resolve the
issue for $10,000 at mediation, but Defendant declined. (Ibid.)
In opposition, Defendant contends the fee requested are unreasonable for a case because
there was nothing extraordinary about this case that settled in 7 months. Defendant requests the
fees incurred by Plaintiffs’ counsel be reduced to a reasonable billing rate per the lodestar
calculation.
In reply, Plaintiffs point out GM’s opposition attacks time entries that Plaintiffs are not
seeking. Plaintiffs contend their rates are reasonable.
Analysis
I. Standard of Law
Under Civil Code section 1794, subdivision (d), “[i]f the buyer prevails in an action under
[the Song-Beverly Act], the buyer shall be allowed by the court to recover as part of the judgment
a sum equal to the aggregate amount of costs and expenses, including attorney’s fees based on
actual time expended, determined by the court to have been reasonably incurred by the buyer in
connection with the commencement and prosecution of such action.”
II. Defendants’ Evidentiary Objections
The Court OVERRULES objections 1, 3, 4 as meritless.
Page 14 of 17
The Court SUSTAINS objection 2 as irrelevant.
III. Merits
The matter of reasonableness of a party's attorney fees is within the sound discretion of
the trial court. (Bruckman v. Parliament Escrow Co. (1989) 190 Cal.App.3d 1051, 1062.) Although
a fee request ordinarily should be documented in great detail, the court is entitled to make its own
evaluation of the reasonable worth of the work done in light of the nature of the case and the
credibility of counsel's declaration, unsubstantiated by time records and billing statements. (See
Weber v. Langholz (1995) 39 Cal.App.4th 1578, 1587; see also Bernardi v. County of Monterey
(2008) 167 Cal.App.4th 1379, 1394.)
A. Lodestar
In determining the reasonable amount of attorney fees, the court first determines a
lodestar figure (time reasonably spent by each biller multiplied by an hourly rate that is reasonable
for each biller.) (Serrant v. Priest (1977) 20 Cal.3d 25, 48.) In exercising its discretion, the Court
may consider all of the facts and the entire procedural history of the case in setting the amount of
a reasonable attorney fee award. (Bernardi, supra, 167 Cal.App.4th 1379, 1394; see also PLCM
Group, Inc. v. Drexler (2000) 22 Cal.4th at 1096 (factors considered in determining the
reasonableness of a party's attorney fees include the nature of the litigation, its difficulty, the
amount involved, the skill required in its handling, the skill employed, the attention given and the
success or failure.).) The court does not need expert testimony to determine the reasonable
amount of a fee award. (PLCM Group, supra, 22 Cal.4th at 1095.)
The matter of reasonableness of a party's attorney fees is within the sound discretion of
the trial court. (Bruckman v. Parliament Escrow Co. (1989) 190 Cal.App.3d 1051, 1062.) Fee
motions should be based on detailed time records. (Crespin v. Shewry (2004) 125 Cal.App.4th
259, 271.) The records should detail crucial information as the types of issues involved, services
performed, numbers of hours, billing rates, etc. (Martino v. Denevi (1986) 182 Cal.App.3d 553,
559.) The court is then entitled to make its own evaluation of the reasonable worth of the work
done in light of the nature of the case and the credibility of counsel's declaration, unsubstantiated
by time records and billing statements. (See Weber v. Langholz (1995) 39 Cal.App.4th 1578,
1587; see also Bernardi v. County of Monterey (2008) 167 Cal.App.4th 1379, 1394.)

i. Reasonable Hourly Rate
A “reasonable” hourly rate is the prevailing rate charged by attorneys of similar skill and
experience in the relevant community. (PLCM Group, supra, 22 Cal.4th at 1095.) The proposed
rate here appears reasonable.
The hourly rates do not appear to be reasonable for Riverside County for Dillavou and
Jacobs. Therefore, the Court reduces the requested rates to $300 and $400 respectively.
Further, Plaintiffs seek 4 hours of unspecified “additional wrap up fees” at $650 per hour.
It is unclear who will be attending the hearing to wrap up the case to justify the hourly rate and
how much time will be spent on each wrap up task. As such, the Court reduces the wrap up
fees to 1.0 hours at $350.00 (strike 3 hours).
ii. Reasonable Hours
The starting point for every fee award is calculating an attorney's services by the time
expended on the case. (Levy v. Toyota Motor Sales, U.S.A., Inc. (1992) 4 Cal.App.4th 807,
815.)
GM argues Plaintiff's fees are unreasonable and excessive with challenges to specific
billing entries.
While this case was filed on 2/18/25, Notice of Settlement of Entire Case was filed on
10/6/25. The Court did not hear any motions during the 8-month pendency of the case.
Duplicate Entries. GM lists entries it believes are duplicate. However, Plaintiffs are not
seeking fees for most of these billing entries, such as those by “AZ”, “LN”, “VP”. Examples 1, 5,
8, 9, 12, 13, 16, and 17 listed by GM in its opposition do appear to be duplicate entries
performed by the paralegals. The Court strikes 1.5 hours.
Excessive Time. GM contends various entries are excessive in time spent. Of the entries
GM disputes, it appears Dillavou's 5.2 hours drafting the fee motion is excessive. Moreover, for
this same entry, it appears there was time billed for the preparation of a declaration on behalf of
Jacobs in support of Plaintiff's instant motion, but no such declaration was filed. The Court
reduces the time spent to 2.0 hours (strike 3.2 hours).
